options.fullText: Research only; change nothing. Use official sources, cite each finding, and separate what's established from what's likely or unknown.
Research the realistic options and compare them side by side, with sources. Don't choose unless asked.
Find the answer from a reliable source, cite it, and stop.

options.shortName: Follow how others already do it
options.fullText: Never reinvent a wheel. Find how established products and libraries already solve this and follow that. Get approval before departing from it.
Check for a well-maintained library before writing something general-purpose.
Build what is needed directly.
Prove one thing works, as small and fast as possible, in throwaway code. State the question first; show the proof; ask for a human check where you can't judge it yourself.
Prove it works with a small clean prototype the real build can grow from.
Reproduce the bug, find the cause with evidence, fix the cause, and add a test that fails without the fix. Change nothing else.
Find the likely cause, fix it, and show the problem is gone.
Review only; change nothing. Check each requirement yourself and report met or not met with evidence, plus defects with file and line.
Read the change and point out anything wrong or risky. Change nothing.
Treat only what you were given as true. Use other files or work only when told you may, and only as told.
Treat as true only what current official sources confirm or what you have proved by running it. Cite where each fact came from.
Use anything in the project or environment that helps.

options.shortName: Do not add or change details
options.fullText:
Do not add or change details when translating user direction or information.

This was clarified when the agent got it wrong twice:
- User said: be brief
- Agent wrote: keep it to one line
  - Wrong
    - User did not restrict length
    - Agent added a limit on its own
- User corrected: never add details or rules I did not state
- Agent wrote the rule as: record in the user's own words
  - Wrong again
    - User did not restrict rewording
    - User only forbade changing or adding detail
      - Less constraining than requiring exact words
- Both mistakes, same mistake
  - A gap
  - Filled with the agent's own detail
  - Presented as if the user had said it

Agents infer and guess far too much. Never add a detail, limit, number, or rule the user did not state. Gaps are named as your own assumption and asked about, or left open. Never quietly turned into a rule.
Fill small gaps sensibly and list every assumption at the end.
Where the instructions are silent, decide for yourself.
Do exactly what was asked, no more. Change nothing outside the scope; report what you notice instead. If something can't be built to spec, stop and ask; never substitute.
Stay in scope. Small related fixes are fine if you list each one.
If something can't be built as specified, build the closest working version and say what differs.
When blocked, stop and ask one question: the question, the context, the options. Don't pick for yourself. Questions that don't block you: decide and note it.

options.shortName: Handle it only if in scope
options.fullText: Resolve a blocker yourself only if you can stay strictly in scope; otherwise stop and ask.
When unsure, decide, keep going, and list your decisions at the end.
Ask whenever you're unsure.

Name things for what they are or do, never for how they're implemented or who uses them (`retry_with_backoff`, not `loop_helper`). Prefer a longer clear name to a short vague one. Never brand internals with the app name.
Short, idiomatic names in the style of the language and framework.
Name things the way the codebase already does.
Build separable pieces as standalone modules: no knowledge of the project using them, a small interface, their own docs and tests.
Split the work into parts with small, explicit interfaces.
Abstract only when there's a second use.
Object-oriented: small single-purpose classes, composition over inheritance.
Functional: pure functions, no mutation, side effects at the edges.
Research the current industry-standard patterns for this problem and use them; say which and why.
Use the patterns the codebase already uses.
Big picture first: build every part as a working stub with its interfaces and tests before filling any in. Filling in never adds new structure.
Build one thin slice end to end, then extend it.
Build it in whatever order makes sense.
Break the work into sprint features, each a standalone tool with its own interface, definition of done, tests and README.
Break the work into small tasks, each done in one sitting.
Do the work as one piece.
No tests.
Test what you've made to ensure it works.
Test first at the module level, with automated tests kept in version control. Finish with real integration tests.
Strict test-first TDD for every behaviour, with automated tests kept in version control.
Specify the format of everything that has one: output, files, docs, reports. Anything left open is named as discretion.
Format things the way the project already does.
Formatting is your call.
Don't alternate asking and working. Research first, then ask all your questions together, one at a time.
Ask questions as they come up.
When there's a choice, make it yourself and say what you chose.
When there's a choice, briefly list the options you can see and say which you'd pick.
When there's a choice, research it first, then present the options with what you found and recommend one. Asking the user is not a substitute for research.
When there's a choice, research it first, then present the options and trade-offs without recommending one.

options.shortName: Research errors, never guess and retry
options.fullText:
When troubleshooting, never fall into a 'try and repeat' loop: failing to research the problem properly and instead testing random guesses with expensive and time-consuming workflows. That can waste hours and hundreds of dollars. You are not authorized to make wild guesses and then run them through CI/CD.

Errors MUST be researched with good generic search terms, NOT niche terms based on your own hypotheses. Searching on your hypothesis is as bad as guessing.
Try quick, cheap experiments first; research if they don't settle it.
Get explicit permission before anything that costs money per use.
Research and prove a fix before any run that costs money per use.
Research and prove a fix, then ask permission before any run that costs money per use.
Use your judgement on paid runs within this limit: [time / usage / cost limit].
No limits on paid runs.
No documentation.
Update existing docs your change makes wrong.
Give everything you build a README: what it is, how to use it, an example.
Document each part: README, interface, and the decisions made and why.
End with: Status / Built / Tests (commands and results) / Deviations / Decisions / Open items.
Respond with headings and short indented bullets. No prose paragraphs.
Respond like slides: short titled sections of 3–5 bullets.
Start with a one- or two-sentence TL;DR.
Give only the answer or result.
Condensed: nested fragments, no filler, no lost facts.
Use stacked PRs; keep working instead of waiting on merges. Have a separate agent review each PR.
One pull request at the end.
Commit directly; no pull requests.
Suggest work that can run in parallel.
One thing at a time.
If there's no repo, suggest one (at least a local one).
No repository.
